item.title: Western Australia’s humpback sightings fell 60%; days later, weakened Southern Ocean seabirds appeared thousands of kilometres away on the country’s east coast
item.description: Unusual whale and seabird sightings in the Southern Ocean suggest changing ocean conditions. Marine heat waves are affecting waters around Australia and Antarctica. These warming events disrupt food webs and push marine life off course. Limited monitoring hinders understanding of these significant ecosystem shifts. Better long-term data is urgently needed to track these accelerating changes.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: Costa Rica scientists placed an AI touchscreen in a wild forest; 16 capuchin monkeys used it for banana rewards
item.description: In a groundbreaking development, scientists created an AI system designed to explore the cognitive functions of capuchin monkeys in the wild. This state-of-the-art system leverages facial recognition and touchscreen interaction to perform automated cognitive tests. Dubbed CapuchinAI, it facilitates the tracking of unique learning and memory traits. Promising results were observed during tests in a Costa Rican forest reserve, providing a scalable approach to studying primate cognition in real-world settings.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: $10k grant helped grow 3,500 hectares of forest protecting Kalgoorlie
item.description: Kalgoorlie-Boulder once suffered severe dust storms due to mining activities. A greening initiative began in the 1970s to combat this environmental problem. Thousands of hectares of forest now protect the city from windblown dust. This long-term project dramatically reduced dust levels over twenty years. The city now enjoys improved air quality and beautified landscapes.

item.title: Nmplol vs Zoil drama explained as Twitch self-gifting controversy turns into ugly public fallout
item.description: Nmplol and Zoil are publicly battling it out after Zoil admitted to anonymously gifting himself 20 Twitch subscriptions to start a Hype Train. The admission led to criticism from Nmplol, leaked Discord messages, and more comments during livestreams from both creators. Here's how the disagreement unfolded, what each streamer said, and why the argument has continued over several days.

item.title: South American frogs are losing their poisonous skin which keeps them safe from predators: Scientists reveal how they could get it back
item.description: Harlequin frogs face extinction as many species decline and some may be extinct. These amphibians are losing their toxic skin defence, leaving them vulnerable to predators. Captive-born frogs lack essential toxins, which are likely produced by skin bacteria in their natural habitat. Scientists are experimenting with feeding toxins to frogs and studying their biology for conservation to protect vital ecosystems and biodiversity.

item.title: Who won Ludwig’s Streamer Games 2026? Complete results, final standings, and winning team
item.description: Ludwig's Streamer Games 2026 wrapped up after two days of competition at USC in Los Angeles. Team Worldwide finished first with 72 points, beating seven other creator teams. Ludwig praised the squad for dominating every event, while the final standings also sparked mixed reactions online. Here's the complete leaderboard, the winning roster, and what Ludwig said after announcing the champions during his livestream.

item.title: Black mamba is the fastest snake on Earth: How it hunts, strikes and captures prey with remarkable efficiency
item.description: Renowned as one of Africa's deadliest inhabitants, the black mamba is a swift and aggressive serpent that can grow to an impressive fourteen feet. Its venom, rich in neurotoxins, results in a fatality rate of nearly one hundred percent if medical intervention is not administered promptly. In many remote regions, the difficulty of obtaining antivenin enhances the danger these snakes present.

item.title: Scientists claim the shrinking Pacific Ocean will lead to the formation of a new supercontinent 'Amasia'
item.description: The Pacific Ocean, which is the largest ocean on Earth, is gradually shrinking due to the convergence of tectonic plates. Subduction zones around its edges are consuming the ocean floor at a rate faster than new material is formed. Scientists estimate that in 200 to 300 million years, the Pacific could entirely close up, pulling continents together to create a new supercontinent.

item.title: Only three Hawaiian producers meet US's organic honey standards; study suggests rule review
item.description: A new study found that organically managed bee colonies on farms in the northeastern US produced honey with pesticide residue levels comparable to certified organic honey. Researchers say current US organic certification rules may be stricter than necessary, but caution that more studies across different regions are needed before any nationwide policy changes.

item.title: Scientists survey Mount Ararat glacier to recover its first ice core
item.description: A German-Turkish research team has completed the first scientific survey of the glacier on Mount Ararat, Turkey's highest peak, to study its potential as a record of climate and human history. Scientists mapped the shrinking ice cap to identify the best site for drilling the mountain's first ice core, hoping it will reveal thousands of years of environmental and archaeological information before melting erases it.

item.title: Raji Doshi, 12, designed an algae system to reduce ocean acidity; now eyes $25,000 science prize
item.description: A young student from Connecticut is a finalist in a science competition for her innovative project. Her project proposes using algae and natural calcium buffers to reduce ocean acidification. This innovative idea could help protect vulnerable marine organisms from acidic conditions. She is competing for a substantial grand prize and valuable scientific mentorship. Her work highlights the significant contributions young minds can make to environmental solutions.

item.title: Meet the General Grant Tree: The world's second-largest tree that became America's only living National Shrine
item.description: The General Grant Tree stands as the world's second-largest tree by volume. It became America's National Christmas Tree in nineteen twenty-six. President Dwight D. Eisenhower declared it a living National Shrine in nineteen fifty-six. This sequoia honors men and women who served the nation. Its size and history make it a remarkable natural landmark.

item.title: Pacific trend raised US Southwest wildfire area 22%, cut Australia’s 19%
item.description: A Pacific Ocean warming trend has impacted wildfire conditions globally. This pattern amplified fire risks in the southwestern United States significantly. Conversely, it eased fire conditions in eastern Australia during the study. Researchers analyzed decades of wildfire and climate data for these findings. Understanding these ocean-climate links can improve future wildfire forecasts.

item.title: Nearly 81 years after Hiroshima, scientists discover a hidden metal alloy created by the atomic bomb blast
item.description: Scientists found a new metallic alloy in Hiroshima shoreline sand. This alloy formed from extreme heat and rapid cooling during the 1945 atomic blast. Researchers identified its unique chemical makeup and crystal structure in microscopic particles. The discovery offers insights into matter behavior under extreme conditions. This finding could inspire future materials science research and nuclear forensics.
